_note: Rewritten to stop defending itself. The previous script kept insisting things were real — 'not simulated', 'nothing is invented', 'for contrast the competing entry' — which nobody asked for and which makes a viewer suspicious who wasn't. Say what it does, in words a non-technical viewer follows, and let the screen carry the proof.

lines.text: When you place a trade on most exchanges, everyone can see it before it happens. Bots watch for big orders, jump in front, and sell back to you at a worse price. You lose money simply because your order was visible. dorr is a trading app on Flare that fixes this by hiding your order until it is too late to exploit.
Let's walk through it as a new user. Empty wallet, no positions, nothing set up.
Trades here are backed by FXRP — that's XRP, bridged onto Flare so it can be used by smart contracts. Since this is a test network, the tokens come from a free faucet.
This button opens Flare's faucet, which hands out test tokens. Our wallet already has some, so let's put them to work.
Connecting the wallet — the same way you would on any crypto app.
Now we move some FXRP into dorr's vault. This is the money we will trade with, and it takes two transactions on Flare: one to approve, one to deposit.
The vault shows what we have. Free is what we can trade with, locked is what is already backing a position.
Here is the trade. We pick how much to risk and how much leverage to use, and the app shows the position size and the price at which we would be liquidated.
And here is the choice that makes dorr different. Public sends your order out in the open, like every other exchange. Private hides it. Let's do both, so you can see the difference.
First, public. Sign the order and send it.
And there it is, on the right, for anyone to read: buy, forty-one FLR, five times leverage, and the wallet that sent it. A bot watching this feed has everything it needs to trade against us.
Here is what that order put on Flare. The vault reserving your money against the position — your wallet, the amount, the time. Anyone can open this and check it.
Now the same trade, private.

Same feed, same moment — and this time all it shows is a string of letters and numbers. That is a fingerprint of the order. It cannot be reversed into the original, so there is nothing for a bot to trade against.

And here is the private order's transaction. Put them side by side: the same kind of record, and neither one names a side, a size, or a price. The chain never saw the difference. The order feed did — the public one was readable while it waited, the private one was a hash.
We can still see our own position — entry price, leverage, and where it would be liquidated. Hidden from everyone else, not from us.

So if nobody can read the order, who matches it? A computer chip that can keep a secret. Our matching engine runs inside a sealed area of an Intel processor, rented from a company called Phala. Software outside that area, including us, cannot look inside it.

And the chip signs a receipt for every batch it settles. That receipt is tied to the exact trades in that batch, so it cannot be reused for a different one. Anyone can check it against Intel's records.

Flare checks it too. Before accepting a settlement, the contract looks up the real market price from Flare's own oracle and rejects anything more than two percent away from it. So even if we wanted to cheat, the chain would stop us.
Now let's attack it ourselves. The same order, run twice — once readable, once hidden — with real fills against the live pool.

With the order readable, the attacker buys ahead of it, the trader fills at a worse price, and the attacker closes out two hundred dollars richer. That money came from the trader. With the order hidden there is only a fingerprint. Twenty-five thousand real attempts to reverse it, none of them land, and the attack cannot even be built: no direction, no size, nothing to get in front of.
The hiding uses a public randomness network that releases a key on a fixed schedule. Until that moment, the key does not exist — so even we cannot open an order early. Watch it try, and fail.
And every order in a batch settles at one shared price. A bot that buys just before you and sells just after gets the same price on both sides, which means it makes nothing.
Here is the vault's history on Flare. Money in from depositors, money out to depositors, and nothing else — because the contract has no way for us to withdraw your funds.
The app has a page that reads all of this live from the running system, so you are never taking our word for the numbers.
It shows the chip is active and signing, and that the operator holds no signing key of its own. It has to ask the sealed chip, every time.

What is not solved yet. We still run the matching engine ourselves, the way most exchanges run a sequencer. Trading depth is built into the app rather than borrowed from a bigger market. And this is a test network with an unaudited contract, so it is not ready for real money.
Every contract, every transaction and the live attestation are linked in the repository, so you can check all of it yourself. Thanks very much for watching.
